exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
exploitedBy.relevance: Directly describes data transmission over unencrypted protocols, matching the risk of unencrypted transport channels.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Network Sniffing
exploitedBy.relevance: Unencrypted transport exposes data to network sniffing attacks where adversaries can capture plaintext traffic.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Downgrade Attack
exploitedBy.relevance: Directly describes forcing negotiation to weaker protocol versions, which is the core risk in weak TLS protocol negotiation.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Weaken Encryption
exploitedBy.relevance: Covers adversary techniques to weaken encryption strength, relevant when TLS negotiation allows weak cipher suites or protocol versions.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
exploitedBy.relevance: Without mutual TLS authentication, adversaries can position themselves between client and server to intercept or manipulate traffic.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
exploitedBy.relevance: Missing mTLS allows attackers to impersonate endpoints; stolen or forged certificates enable bypassing certificate-based authentication.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Protocol or Service Impersonation
exploitedBy.relevance: Absence of mutual authentication enables service impersonation where a malicious endpoint masquerades as a legitimate one.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Install Root Certificate
exploitedBy.relevance: Installing rogue root certificates is a primary technique to bypass TLS certificate validation by making fraudulent certificates appear trusted.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Transmitted Data Manipulation
exploitedBy.relevance: Without message integrity controls, adversaries can manipulate transmitted data in transit, directly matching this risk.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Application Access Token
exploitedBy.relevance: Captured tokens can be replayed to gain unauthorized access, directly representing the replay attack threat.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Steal Application Access Token
exploitedBy.relevance: Stolen tokens lacking replay protection can be reused by attackers to impersonate legitimate sessions.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Application Exhaustion Flood
exploitedBy.relevance: Without rate limiting, application-layer flood attacks can exhaust resources, directly exploiting the absence of transport-level controls.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Service Exhaustion Flood
exploitedBy.relevance: Missing rate limiting exposes services to exhaustion flood attacks that overwhelm transport-layer service capacity.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Network Boundary Bridging
exploitedBy.relevance: BGP hijacking can bridge network boundaries by rerouting traffic across network perimeters through malicious autonomous systems.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Protocol Tunneling
exploitedBy.relevance: Insecure backend communication channels can be exploited using protocol tunneling to bypass security controls between the gateway and backend.

exploitedBy.label: MitreAttackTechnique
exploitedBy.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
exploitedBy.relevance: Unprotected API gateway-to-backend legs can be leveraged for data exfiltration using alternative protocols that bypass monitoring.
